full_text:
Interviewer:	Did you start in July?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	And do you finish in July as well?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Okay. [name] and [name] have obviously already told me, but, can you tell me a bit about the company that you’re working for?

Subject:	I’m afraid not, we asked if we could get you to …

Interviewer:	Only like really simply.

Subject:	Yeah, um, basically it’s a multi national company, um, so we’re based here, but we get to travel to other sites as well, so it’s got different places and I’m – I’m based in the packaging team so, um, yeah, that’s basically it. We make – well, we make [product] here.

Interviewer:	Okay. What is their confidentiality thing? Is that so I won’t go and steal your designs?

Subject:	No, it’s not just the designs. Um, people just have stuff lying about on desks and they’re really like the big competitor’s [company] and they’re just really, really, um, het up about their company secrets and stuff and we asked them if you could, um, could get a confidentiality form for you but she was worried that because you’re doing a post grad thing you might write about the company in your thesis or whatever.

Interviewer:	We won’t name you and we won’t name the company even in this stuff so, it’s confidential from our point of view as well.

Subject:	Oh brilliant, okay. They just, honestly they’re so funny about it. I mean I – I’m allowed to talk to you on a sort of top level but I can’t tell you exactly what I’m working on and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yeah, that’s fine. Okay. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Pretty, um, equal really. I mean like I don’t – I haven’t noticed any – had any trouble and I think it’s pretty much 50:50 men and women in here as far as – as far as I’ve noticed. And, um, looking at the placement students, certainly here there’s more girls than there are boys anyway, so, um, I think it’s pretty even. The only thing on my team, um, there’s only two – there’s – people on my team who work here there’s eight of us and there’s only two of us who are female and one of them, she’s pregnant – not me – so she won’t be here for much longer either, so, I mean that’s – but overall it’s quite mixed.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that your degree so far has been useful to the work that you’re doing now?

Subject:	It is, like it’s quite nice when you do something and you think oh, I’ve actually learnt this on my degree, because I'm doing, um, I’m visiting quite a lot of, um, suppliers for plastic packaging and they do sort of injection moulding and so I’ve looked around the factories at the machines and obviously I’ve done – used the same machines in my department, so it’s nice to sort of recognise it and go oh, my whole degree hasn’t been a waste of time. But I’m not doing a particularly design y – I'm doing packaging design but, um, within the company we don’t do so much front line design, it’s more of, um, adapting ideas we’ve already got and stuff, so…

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anything that you wish you had learnt before you started the placement?

Subject:	Um, I think it’s just getting an experience like this you don’t know how to prepare yourself for it anyway so you’re always going to be – take you a while to settle in and I just found things like – I definitely feel like I’ve learnt so much all ready, but whenever I give a presentation or anything I just write reams and reams and since then I’ve been told, you know, just put a few key points, and things like that like maybe I could have learnt before. 

Interviewer:	Did you do any presentation stuff at uni?

Subject:	We did do a few but it was normally in groups and stuff, um, and it was – it was just not so – not so formal and maybe it would be better to actually have a, because you – at the end of the day you know you’re always just presenting to the people you know and so it’s not – you never really get that scared.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

Subject:	Um, I guess, because we worked in the workshops and stuff, they were quite keen on like making sure we had to wear like safety boots and stuff and, um, make sure we were all dressed and we all had to have like a workshop, um, trial thing before we were allowed to just go in there and work off our own backs, so I guess they did do a bit.

Interviewer:	Did you do any health and safety stuff for when you got to work?

Subject:	Oh right, the sort of stuff I might need to know here?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	Would that have been helpful or have you learnt enough since you got here?

Subject:	I just think – I think it’s kind of place specific. I don’t think it’s something they could teach you. It’s like, well, like you’ve seen on the video on your way in, it’s all about cans and cans going round factories, which obviously they can’t teach you about stuff like that at uni, so…

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think the University could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Um, no, I think it’s been – because I think – because the company are quite – have had lots of placement students before they know exactly what to expect of us and certainly in my job they’ve, um, they – they had a placement student from [university] doing my course as well before me. I took over from here like last year, so they knew exactly what I knew already, so it was quite smooth and they knew what they had to teach me, and so it was like I’ve had all the help I’ve needed. I haven’t – it doesn’t – it’s not like I've been thrown in at the deep end. I think maybe like from the company’s point of view it’s because they know that they don’t expect too much of us straight away, so it doesn’t matter what I’ve learnt.

Interviewer:	Okay. Before you started the placement did the University or your Department say what they expected you to get from the placement?

Subject:	It’s always been quite clear because I was never – because I wasn’t too keen on doing a really design y placement anyway and I was always a bit worried that I’d get a placement which wasn’t that related and they’d be a bit funny about it, but they’ve always been just saying that it’s actually the experience of work, it doesn’t really – it doesn’t matter so much what you’re doing it’s just the experience of being in a workplace even if you’re not doing an industrial design, um, job, it’s still going to be of benefit to you.

Interviewer:	Okay. How have you found the transition from education to work?

Subject:	Quite easy; it’s been nice actually. Like it’s obviously totally different. When you’re at work you have like, um, you’ve got, um, work to do in the evenings and stuff, and here you can go home at five o’clock and forget about it. That is really nice and it’s nice to earn money as well.

Interviewer:	Have you had to face any new issues at work, like office politics and working with different people and stuff like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I had, um, quite a big issue, after I’d been working here about two months my manager left, er, she changed jobs and because obviously I’m a student, I’m sort of – you have to be directly supervised so by her changing jobs my placement was sort of, it was apparently coming to an end. Obviously they – they’d made a promise to me it’s going to be a placement for a year and they couldn’t foresee this before I started working here, so, um, the best option for the company was to relocate me to France and, um, work for – so I could do the same job basically as I was doing before, because I was enjoying my job and they were happy with the work I was doing, but it was just that they weren’t – she’s gone on a nine month placement so they weren’t going to replace her. Um, so basically it was a bit – that was quite – it was the kind of decision I haven’t had to make before. It was a bit of a big decision, like oh, do I want to go to France, I don’t speak the language, um, go and work with people I don’t know when I’ve been working here for a few months and I’ve got on with everyone really well and I’ve got a house here and blah, blah, blah. But, um, in the end it turned out that after a few weeks of like trying to decide it turned out the best job was going to be for me to stay here anyway, so there wasn’t really a decision to make in the end, but it definitely provoked thought and stuff.

Interviewer:	Okay. Did you go and see anyone for advice or anything like that?

Subject:	Um, the guy from France came over here to see me, um, which – that was the kind of thing – the next step was going to be for me to visit because I was going ‘I can’t really decide until I’ve seen the place’, um, but just before I was going to go and visit it all sort of became apparent that I could stay here, so it was good.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all?

Subject:	No, I think it’s totally different. Just the whole lifestyle, you know, working nine until five, at university you get like a couple of hours tuition a week or whatever, it’s much more working off your own back. I don’t know, obviously you’re still working off your own back here, I’m not being supervised the whole time, but it’s the whole – the working environment is that everyone’s just getting on with stuff in the same – the same hours of the day, whereas at university you might not get up until 12 or whatever and… it is quite different.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Um, I suppose at work your goals are probably more long term. I mean things that I’m – projects that I’m working on aren’t going to be completed for three or four years, whereas at university, you know, your project’s going to last a couple of weeks or whatever, and it’s much more… you’re working, yeah, you’re working for a specific date. In here, projects are much more open ended, they could get stopped and started at any time.

Interviewer:	How do you find that, when things can go on for three or four years and you won’t see it through to the end, does that…?

Subject:	Yeah, I think, because I haven’t been here that long I haven’t found it too bad yet, but it’s definitely something that the girl who I took over from said to me like it’s hard because you’re working – the project’s obviously you’re going to develop a new dog or cat food first, then you’re going to develop the packaging, then you’re going to put it out as a promotion, then you’re going to properly launch it, so whenever you’re working on anything it’s not going to happen for a few years and she said it’s quite frustrating when you’ve done all this work and then maybe the business hasn’t got enough money to carry it on any more or, you know, you never know and you just have – you know, if someone turns round and says, ‘This project isn’t running any more’ you’d have to get on with it, you can’t go, ‘Oh no, please can you carry it on, I’ve put some work into it’. Um, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do the company have a structure or programme in place for the placement students?

Subject:	Yeah. It’s like, um, you’re supposed to have, like, because there’s a lot of us over all the sites, there’s 50 of us all together, um, so every month we’re supposed to have something. So like last month we went to [place] which is one of the other sites and they – the students there told us what they did, showed us around their site and, um, like next month instead of a visit next month we’re having a presentation skills training, and there’s always – there’s always like training or a visit somewhere each month and then there’s like, there’s goals along the way. Like, um, in January we’re supposed to have appraisals for our half-year, so we set our targets for the rest of the year and things like that, sort of stop off points.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think those things are a good idea then or do you think they could be improved at all?

Subject:	I think it’s a good idea because it’s everyone at the moment everyone in the business is going through exactly the same thing so it kind of makes us more included, like we’re the same as everyone else, and it checks that you’re still doing – because I think it’s quite easy to sort of wander off and not – sort of lose direction of what you’re doing, so it checks you’re still on track.

Interviewer:	Okay. What does your own role in the company involve? What can you tell me about it?

Subject:	Yeah, I can tell you, basically, well, I was in packaging innovation; I'm now in packaging development, so I do similar things. So one of the brands in the business will say, um, ‘We want a new package for this product we’ve got’ and, um, it’ll come to me in innovation, so I just come up with any new crazy ideas that I can, or, you know, different new ways of, um, having a package, and then I normally make prototypes of those packages and maybe take them to consumer testing and then if it’s successful the package would go on and get developed by someone else and, um, hopefully hit the shops.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s quite exciting.

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is that what you expected you would be doing before you started?

Subject:	To be honest, I had no idea at all. I came and visited once before I started just for a day, um, well, not even a day, like a couple of hours in the afternoon, just met my manager and had a walk round, which was good, it kind of put my mind at rest a bit, and, um, yeah, so I knew vaguely but they couldn’t, because of this whole confidentiality thing they couldn’t really tell me until I got here what I was going to be doing, but, um, yeah, it’s perfect, it’s absolutely fine, because I feel like I've got – I’m doing a little bit related to the course but it’s nice, it’s not – it’s not the same, it’s like…

Interviewer:	Yeah, still learning loads of stuff.

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Definitely and certainly since my job’s changed, um, like because my new manager’s sort of acquired me, he never went and recruited me like my old manager did, he’s not had a student before and so it’s a lot more real the stuff I'm doing. These are projects that he’s had sat at the side waiting for someone to have time to do them on his team and now he says, ‘Right, well if Rebecca means to come and work for me then this is what she can do’ and it’s really exciting. It’s good. It’s real, it’s like hopefully something you’ll get in the shops.

Interviewer:	Wow. Do you feel like the company have been supportive of you then?

Subject:	Yeah, I had, well like I say, I had some trouble when I was asked to relocate to France, because basically my manager, because she was – she applied for this nine month secondment, they do it within the business so you can change your role just for nine months, and she didn’t tell me she’d applied because she didn’t know if she’d get it or not, but when she got it it was the day before she was going on holiday for three weeks, so she sort of said to me, ‘Oh Rebecca, I need to talk to you quickly’, and sort of said, ‘Right, I’m leaving my job, um, can you have a think about what you’d like to get out of this year and we’ll try and accommodate you. Think about it. Okay, I’m going on holiday’. So I was a bit sort of – a bit lost, didn’t know what to do really for a few weeks and because she went on holiday it was left for three weeks just for me to think about it, and it turned out nothing was getting done and it was just stressing me out quite a lot. And in the end one day I came in and I was like, ‘Oh what’s going on?’ and after that everyone was really supportive and they were like, ‘Look, this is our problem, not yours. It’s our fault she’s leaving, we need to do everything we can to accommodate you’. So we all sat down and I said what the kind of things I wanted to be doing and everyone, like my new manager said, ‘Right, I’ve got this project you could do, which is something you could do’, so they were all really good in the end.

Interviewer:	Do you wish you had said something earlier then?

Subject:	Definitely, yeah, definitely. It went on, because there was the whole three weeks she was on holiday, it probably went on for at least another three weeks after that as well, of everyone – I think they were expecting me to say like, ‘This is what I want to do’, either go to France or stay in England, and I was waiting for them to say, ‘Right, this is how we’ll help you to make your decision’. No one was actually doing anything, so it’s definitely something I’ve learnt is, you know, I just need to get on with it and say.

Interviewer:	Okay. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	I’ve really enjoyed it. And before I wasn’t sure like I haven’t been – obviously I’ve only been here six months or so, but before I didn’t know what I wanted to do after I graduate but I’m definitely thinking now that I’ll apply for the graduate training scheme, because I’ve just really enjoyed – I don’t mean necessarily here, but just the whole like structured thing and I feel like I’ve learnt so much anyway I wouldn’t mind going straight into a job and doing a similar thing after university. 

Interviewer:	Okay. What have been the best and worst things about the placement so far?

Subject:	Um, so the worst thing was the sort of upheaval, expected to move to France or whatever, but the best thing has been I feel like I’ve got real responsibility and my project’s real and I’ve – I’ve been able to travel quite a lot, which I wasn’t even expecting, so… I’ve been to Holland and I’ve been to Germany and, um, I’ve been lots of places around the UK as well, so it’s really nice. It’s like – I feel like I’ve just learnt a lot just from doing that, so…

Interviewer:	Excellent. Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

Subject:	Um, well, one thing I’ve got to do is my dissertation and I haven’t thought what I’m going to write it on or anything like that, so that’s something I’ve got to do soon, obviously I haven’t done so far. But, um, apart from the whole experience of things I just feel like I’ve learnt so much already I’d quite happily walk out tomorrow and, you know, be happy with what I’ve learnt, because just the whole, just being here and getting involved in everything I think it just – it’s really helped.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that there are any drawbacks at all to doing a placement?

Subject:	I really can’t think of any. I mean like some of my friends are in their final – final year now doing my course and she said to me that just the people who come back from placement are just totally separate from everyone else and they just – they just get on, and she’s a really conscientious girl or she’s always the most conscientious person I’ve ever known, she just said that you can just see they’re so used to being in work and stuff they just get on with everything, like they just – they’re totally separate and they don’t mix with the other people because no one can understand – everyone’s going ‘Oh we’re just going back to bed for another two hours and then we’ll start this project’ and they’re having meetings, and she said, ‘Oh, you’re going to find it so useful next year’ and, you know, she said that as someone who would never have done a placement, but she said that to me, so… It just – I can’t – I just feel like it will help me so much if I’m going to go for graduate schemes as well. I feel like I know so much more about business and stuff.

Interviewer:	You’d recommend other people go on placement or whatever?

Subject:	Definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

Subject:	Um, probably like some of my skills have changed. Um, like I found when I first started I found it quite hard to like ring up people in other countries and just be like, ‘Oh hi, I'm Rebecca’ and start chatting to them, but you’re just expected to and that was something my first manager sort of gave me feedback on. She was like, ‘You’ve just got to get on with it and ring them up’ and so I think I’m probably a bit more confident and, um, but like socially we’re still students really, we all live together and we still act like students, so it’s kind of – it’s probably like that I haven’t changed much, but, um…

Interviewer:	Have you moved here as well?

Subject:	Yeah. So there’s nine of us who are placement students living here. We’ve got two houses, we live next door to each other, so it’s kind of – it’s kind of like being students, which is nice.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you are treated as equally as the other placement students?

Subject:	It’s difficult because we’re all doing different jobs and so like you’ve spoken to [name] and [name] who are on the same course as me but we do totally different things here and, um, I feel – I just think I’ve been quite lucky because – because like I say, everyone else’s managers have had students before but my manager hasn’t and so he’s treating me more like, um, an associate, so that’s why I’ve got to travel – travel and stuff, because, um, he doesn’t realise he shouldn’t spend that much money on me. So it’s probably – it’s hard to compare how we’re treated. Everyone is – everyone – hopefully everyone enjoys it but we’re all doing such different things it’s really hard to compare.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that you’re probably treated more like a permanent member of staff than the other students?

Subject:	I feel – I wouldn’t say more than the other ones, but like with the projects that I’m doing it’s more necessary for me to travel than it is for, say, [name] because she does a lot of laboratory work here, whereas I need to visit suppliers or whatever and they might be abroad, but that’s my project and her project doesn’t entail that so she doesn’t – but maybe I don’t know, because she doesn’t – it might seem to her like, um, oh I get to go on all these trips but it’s because it’s related to my project, it’s not because I'm more important than her at all. Like we’re all equal.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. Have you found it an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement with you?

Subject:	Definitely an advantage, it’s really nice. It’s like it’s so nice to have everyone in the same situation and just have – obviously you get on with everyone in your team and stuff, but to have other people the same age as you and, um, you know, to go and meet up with at lunch time and to find out what they’re doing and… if there are other people you can ask them questions without like feeling stupid, because we’re all in the same situation so… and obviously to live with and just to socialise with it’s nice.

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you had to do much team work?

Subject:	Yeah, um, when I first started working here we were in – there was just really a team of two of us and I worked alongside my manager pretty much all the time. So, we’d design things and then we’d make the models together, just like work together pretty much all the time. And with this new project, um, I’m working more by myself, I’m not so much supervised, but I’ve had to go to lots of different members of the business, like all over the country – all over Europe and get like their expertise on different areas because obviously they know, they’ve been here a lot longer than me and they know more about different areas, so yeah, I think I’ve had to do quite a lot.

Interviewer:	How would you describe your overall experiences of group work, kind of good or bad?

Subject:	It’s really useful for me because, like I say, I’ve been here six months and you’re never going to – as much – as hard as you try you’re never going to learn everything about the business, so, um, just people, they’re just really helpful really.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone that you’ve particularly liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	Um, no, everyone’s been really nice. I think the thing that I’ve found is that no one will help you unless you sort of help them back. So you can’t just send someone an email and ask them to do some research for you or whatever; you need to say, ‘This is what I’ve found out, hopefully it will help your project’ and then ‘Can you help me with this?’ I think that’s quite important to do because everyone’s so busy they don’t have time just to answer everyone’s questions, they like to get – the like to see something or, you know, be updated on what you’re doing or whatever just to – before they help you.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. How do you think that teamwork in the work place compares to teamwork at uni?

Subject:	It’s quite different because, um, definitely at uni you’ve already met – you know everyone, whereas here quite often you’ve got to ring someone up and you’ve got to talk to them when you’ve never even met them and you’ve got to have a relationship without meeting them for ages or have a relationship over a video conference or whatever. It’s not – it’s quite different, but I mean the same – I think working together’s the same, it’s just you’re not so familiar with each other.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. Have you got a mentor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that having a mentor’s a good idea?

Subject:	Um, I don’t know. I think – I think the reason that I’ve got him is supposed to be for, um, if I’ve got a problem with my own manager that I’m supposed to go and talk to him. But I’ve found that because I’ve spent so much more time with people on my team and stuff he’s not actually in my team, but I actually just never go and talk to him because I’d rather talk to people who I know. So, it’s a nice idea to have someone to go to, but I think you’ve got to have – you’ve got – I should have really made an effort to meet him and get to know him rather than wait until something crops up and then go and see him because it’s just like talking to anyone really.

Interviewer:	So would you say that even though you’ve got an official mentor you treat the other people in your team as mentors?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, definitely. Like when, um, I was supposed to be going to France and stuff, I spoke to my official mentor once and that was the first time I’d ever spoken to him because (inaudible) the business and I spoke to people on my team like every day almost, so…

Interviewer:	Okay. What do you think are the benefits and drawbacks of having a mentor?

Subject:	Well, like the drawbacks for me is I kind of get mixed signals because he’s on a similar – like because your mentor’s supposed to be someone who’s on a sort of similar level to your manger, so obviously he knows like the business and he’s quite high up and so he’s sort of like, ‘Oh well I think’, you know, I’ll show him my project and stuff, ‘Oh I think this would be a good idea’ when, you know, you’ve already got direction from someone else. So you kind of get mixed signals a bit, but it is nice to have someone to go to if you need to, like, you know, because my manager travels quite a lot, if he’s not here then I will go to my mentor and just run things past him just because I know he’s got experience and…

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model?

Subject:	Um, I don’t know, because we get – sometimes we get spoken to by like really high people who are high up in the company, which is, I suppose it’s supposed to like inspire us, but it doesn’t really inspire me because they just seem to work really hard and yeah, they like earn a load of money, but I just sort of think it’s not really worth it if you’re going to be working like 24/7. So, I don’t really look up to them. It’s nice, I think it’s – definitely if you’re going to do something you enjoy it’s nice to get high up in a business or whatever, but I just wouldn’t bother if it’s too much work. Like life’s too short.

Interviewer:	Okay. Has anyone from uni been to visit you yet?

Subject:	Um, in work?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Oh, a tutor? Yeah, he has.

Interviewer:	Did they tell you what the purpose of the visit was?

Subject:	No, he’s a bit of a strange man. He came in and he filled – he checked we were writing log books, which we’re supposed to be doing, um, but he met – there’s six of us here from [university], he just met us all at once. We all just sat – we sat round a table in one of these rooms. He basically just asked what we were doing, whether we liked our jobs or not, if we did it was fine, if we didn’t, well, he said, ‘Well, just get on with it because it’s a good experience’ and then he went home.

Interviewer:	So, if you did have any problems would you be happy to go to him?

Subject:	No. He wouldn’t bother. Certainly, like I think some people just said a few things about how they weren’t doing jobs very related to their courses or whatever and he just said, ‘Well, my first job was on a ship where I had to work 12 hours of the day, blah, blah, blah. So don’t ever say you’ve got it bad, just get on with it.’

Interviewer:	So it didn’t feel like he was very supportive?

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is there anyone else that you’d go to at uni if you did have any problems?

Subject:	Um, my tutor’s quite nice, but I think at the end of the day there’s not really – I can’t really – I wouldn’t really expect University to do anything. It’s kind of if I’m at work it’s my problem here and, you know, if I was going to leave the job then I’d leave the job, you know, without – you know, if I felt that strongly about the job then I wouldn’t worry about the University getting involved, I’d just get on with it myself, I think.

Interviewer:	Okay, do you know if uni or here have a complaints procedure if you had any serious problems?

Subject:	Here have, I don’t know about uni, I presume they have. Like there’s – there’s a lady that we’ve all been introduced to who you can go to here, um, in human resources who you can go and talk to if you’ve got a problem and they’ll try and sort it out.

Interviewer:	Do you think that that should have been like made clearer to you at uni?

Subject:	Probably, yeah. I hadn’t even thought of it, to be honest.

Interviewer:	How to go about finding out about stuff really?

Subject:	Yeah. Well I presume you’d just contact the placements guy but like I say he’s a bit funny, so… Yeah, it’s not been made clear.

Interviewer:	Okay. Are there appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. Um, like, do you mean sort of like…

Interviewer:	Basically, the reason that I’m asking is because we’re interviewing engineers and stuff as well and some of them are working on building sites and there aren’t women’s toilets and they have like safety clothing that doesn’t fit them and stuff like that.

Subject:	Yeah, no, the women’s toilets are really nice and they’ve got like about a million mirrors and they’ve got sofas in them and stuff, so I think we’re treated quite well.

Interviewer:	Have there been any occasions when you think that your gender has determined reactions you’ve got, or the outcome of events or anything?

Subject:	I don’t think so. I always worry, well, I don’t worry about my gender, when I go and see suppliers I’m worried I just look really young, because I don’t tell them I’m a student they just get really confused, thinking why am I so young and why I’m there, but I’ve never – I’ve never really thought as gender being – because like there’s people around me who are quite high up who are female it doesn’t ever seem – you’d never think that there’d be an issue really.

Interviewer:	I think you did mention this earlier, but at the minute do you think that you want a career in design and technology?

Subject:	Um, yeah, I was saying that I want to do like graduate or something, but like what I’m doing at the moment isn’t particularly design and technology and I’d be quite happy just to – and seeing like the different things people do it’s really interesting around the company, so I wouldn’t be applying specifically for design and technology I don’t think. I’d just go for, like the graduate schemes here you do six months in different jobs, you keep switching round, so I think that’s the kind of thing I’d like to do, get a taste of everything.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed since doing the placement?

Subject:	Yeah. I had no idea what I wanted to do before I started. Um, I still don’t know what – what jobs specifically I’d want to do, but I definitely think it’d be worthwhile me going on a graduate scheme, so…

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after uni?

Subject:	Yeah, it will, but I don’t think it will help my final year at uni because I'm not doing – I feel like I'm getting a bit out of touch with what – the stuff I did at uni. I think it will be hard to go back in there and – for the last year and get motivated again.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think you’ll be able to use what you’ve learnt for your final year project or anything?

Subject:	Probably not. It’s not very – it’s not very related, so that’s why I think I’ll find it hard.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Okay. Would you work for [company] if they offered you a job when you graduated?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. It would depend what it is and where it is and stuff, well, actually I don’t really mind where it is, but it would depend what the job is because there’s so much different stuff going on.

Interviewer:	If it was similar to what you were doing now?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay. These are some questions that I asked you in the last interview, just to see if your views have changed at all since working, so what five words would you now use to describe either design and technology generally or specifically what you’re doing?
Subject:	Okay, so I can choose either/or?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Okay, so what I’m doing now is probably easier. So, it’s creative, but it’s not – yeah, so it’s creative, so I’m still being creative, but it’s not like really arty, so that’s not really a word. Um, it’s enlightening because I get to go lots of different places, yeah, so it’s exciting, and I think it’s quite, I guess like broadening because I get to like learn about lots of different things I didn’t learn about before.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so varied?

Subject:	Yeah, varied, yeah. That’s four, so I’ll try and think of another one.

Interviewer:	It’s okay if you can’t.

Subject:	Is that okay?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think now that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated area or can’t you really answer that properly, working here, because it’s quite even?

Subject:	It’s, because it’s quite even I don’t think, because definitely when I think, I probably said last time, when I went into university because they don’t have very many females on the course, um, I felt like I kind of just got in by default because they needed more females, but I definitely don’t feel like that here. Like I, you know, they interviewed us fairly.

Interviewer:	You feel like you’ve got it because you deserve it rather than…

Subject:	Yeah, rather than just coming in because ‘Oh, we need to make up the numbers’, yeah.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled into the industry?

Subject:	More women should be encouraged into?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Um, I don’t – I don’t really see… I don’t think that, no, I don’t think there’s any kind of real problem. It’s probably – it might just be unlucky that there’s more males than females on my team at the moment, but certainly my old manager was female, she’s now left the team so there will have been more. I think it’s kind of swings and roundabouts; I don’t think they need to be particularly encouraged more. Um, I think it’s quite even.

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think there’s any particular reason why the industry generally is quite male dominated but here isn’t so much? Is it the company’s attitude or…?

Subject:	Yeah, I don’t know. Like when I went to Germany last week I came back on, because it was a midweek flight it was obviously a kind of business flight and I was the only female on the whole plane.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yeah. Because I really – I noticed that because I wasn’t dressed up very smart and everyone was dressed up smart and they were kind of looking at me like, you know, what are you doing here? And I was just sort of thinking this is quite bizarre because you don’t – you never feel like you’re, um, that things are – I don’t ever really feel like it’s unequal anywhere but then why are there so many businessmen on this plane and just me? I don’t know why that is. I don’t know why it’s male dominated, but maybe it probably all comes down to women looking after kids.

Interviewer:	Have [company] got equal opportunities policies and I think [name] said you can work like flexible hours and stuff like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so.

Interviewer:	So that sort of helps, I suppose, with child care issues.

Subject:	Yeah, as far as I know, I think, I mean definitely like the lady on my team is pregnant so she’s been going off to all her appointments and everything, like I think they’re quite flexible, as far as I know.

Interviewer:	Yeah, okay. That’s everything, thank you very much.

Subject:	Oh, brilliant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you start in July?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you finish in July as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. [name] and [name] have obviously already told me, but, can you tell me a bit about the company that you’re working for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m afraid not, we asked if we could get you to …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Only like really simply.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, um, basically it’s a multi national company, um, so we’re based here, but we get to travel to other sites as well, so it’s got different places and I’m – I’m based in the packaging team so, um, yeah, that’s basically it. We make – well, we make [product] here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What is their confidentiality thing? Is that so I won’t go and steal your designs?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it’s not just the designs. Um, people just have stuff lying about on desks and they’re really like the big competitor’s [company] and they’re just really, really, um, het up about their company secrets and stuff and we asked them if you could, um, could get a confidentiality form for you but she was worried that because you’re doing a post grad thing you might write about the company in your thesis or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: We won’t name you and we won’t name the company even in this stuff so, it’s confidential from our point of view as well.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh brilliant, okay. They just, honestly they’re so funny about it. I mean I – I’m allowed to talk to you on a sort of top level but I can’t tell you exactly what I’m working on and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, that’s fine. Okay. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Pretty, um, equal really. I mean like I don’t – I haven’t noticed any – had any trouble and I think it’s pretty much 50:50 men and women in here as far as – as far as I’ve noticed. And, um, looking at the placement students, certainly here there’s more girls than there are boys anyway, so, um, I think it’s pretty even. The only thing on my team, um, there’s only two – there’s – people on my team who work here there’s eight of us and there’s only two of us who are female and one of them, she’s pregnant – not me – so she won’t be here for much longer either, so, I mean that’s – but overall it’s quite mixed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that your degree so far has been useful to the work that you’re doing now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is, like it’s quite nice when you do something and you think oh, I’ve actually learnt this on my degree, because I'm doing, um, I’m visiting quite a lot of, um, suppliers for plastic packaging and they do sort of injection moulding and so I’ve looked around the factories at the machines and obviously I’ve done – used the same machines in my department, so it’s nice to sort of recognise it and go oh, my whole degree hasn’t been a waste of time. But I’m not doing a particularly design y – I'm doing packaging design but, um, within the company we don’t do so much front line design, it’s more of, um, adapting ideas we’ve already got and stuff, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anything that you wish you had learnt before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think it’s just getting an experience like this you don’t know how to prepare yourself for it anyway so you’re always going to be – take you a while to settle in and I just found things like – I definitely feel like I’ve learnt so much all ready, but whenever I give a presentation or anything I just write reams and reams and since then I’ve been told, you know, just put a few key points, and things like that like maybe I could have learnt before.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do any presentation stuff at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We did do a few but it was normally in groups and stuff, um, and it was – it was just not so – not so formal and maybe it would be better to actually have a, because you – at the end of the day you know you’re always just presenting to the people you know and so it’s not – you never really get that scared.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I guess, because we worked in the workshops and stuff, they were quite keen on like making sure we had to wear like safety boots and stuff and, um, make sure we were all dressed and we all had to have like a workshop, um, trial thing before we were allowed to just go in there and work off our own backs, so I guess they did do a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do any health and safety stuff for when you got to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh right, the sort of stuff I might need to know here?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would that have been helpful or have you learnt enough since you got here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I just think – I think it’s kind of place specific. I don’t think it’s something they could teach you. It’s like, well, like you’ve seen on the video on your way in, it’s all about cans and cans going round factories, which obviously they can’t teach you about stuff like that at uni, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think the University could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no, I think it’s been – because I think – because the company are quite – have had lots of placement students before they know exactly what to expect of us and certainly in my job they’ve, um, they – they had a placement student from [university] doing my course as well before me. I took over from here like last year, so they knew exactly what I knew already, so it was quite smooth and they knew what they had to teach me, and so it was like I’ve had all the help I’ve needed. I haven’t – it doesn’t – it’s not like I've been thrown in at the deep end. I think maybe like from the company’s point of view it’s because they know that they don’t expect too much of us straight away, so it doesn’t matter what I’ve learnt.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Before you started the placement did the University or your Department say what they expected you to get from the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s always been quite clear because I was never – because I wasn’t too keen on doing a really design y placement anyway and I was always a bit worried that I’d get a placement which wasn’t that related and they’d be a bit funny about it, but they’ve always been just saying that it’s actually the experience of work, it doesn’t really – it doesn’t matter so much what you’re doing it’s just the experience of being in a workplace even if you’re not doing an industrial design, um, job, it’s still going to be of benefit to you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How have you found the transition from education to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Quite easy; it’s been nice actually. Like it’s obviously totally different. When you’re at work you have like, um, you’ve got, um, work to do in the evenings and stuff, and here you can go home at five o’clock and forget about it. That is really nice and it’s nice to earn money as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to face any new issues at work, like office politics and working with different people and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I had, um, quite a big issue, after I’d been working here about two months my manager left, er, she changed jobs and because obviously I’m a student, I’m sort of – you have to be directly supervised so by her changing jobs my placement was sort of, it was apparently coming to an end. Obviously they – they’d made a promise to me it’s going to be a placement for a year and they couldn’t foresee this before I started working here, so, um, the best option for the company was to relocate me to France and, um, work for – so I could do the same job basically as I was doing before, because I was enjoying my job and they were happy with the work I was doing, but it was just that they weren’t – she’s gone on a nine month placement so they weren’t going to replace her. Um, so basically it was a bit – that was quite – it was the kind of decision I haven’t had to make before. It was a bit of a big decision, like oh, do I want to go to France, I don’t speak the language, um, go and work with people I don’t know when I’ve been working here for a few months and I’ve got on with everyone really well and I’ve got a house here and blah, blah, blah. But, um, in the end it turned out that after a few weeks of like trying to decide it turned out the best job was going to be for me to stay here anyway, so there wasn’t really a decision to make in the end, but it definitely provoked thought and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Did you go and see anyone for advice or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the guy from France came over here to see me, um, which – that was the kind of thing – the next step was going to be for me to visit because I was going ‘I can’t really decide until I’ve seen the place’, um, but just before I was going to go and visit it all sort of became apparent that I could stay here, so it was good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think it’s totally different. Just the whole lifestyle, you know, working nine until five, at university you get like a couple of hours tuition a week or whatever, it’s much more working off your own back. I don’t know, obviously you’re still working off your own back here, I’m not being supervised the whole time, but it’s the whole – the working environment is that everyone’s just getting on with stuff in the same – the same hours of the day, whereas at university you might not get up until 12 or whatever and… it is quite different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I suppose at work your goals are probably more long term. I mean things that I’m – projects that I’m working on aren’t going to be completed for three or four years, whereas at university, you know, your project’s going to last a couple of weeks or whatever, and it’s much more… you’re working, yeah, you’re working for a specific date. In here, projects are much more open ended, they could get stopped and started at any time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you find that, when things can go on for three or four years and you won’t see it through to the end, does that…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think, because I haven’t been here that long I haven’t found it too bad yet, but it’s definitely something that the girl who I took over from said to me like it’s hard because you’re working – the project’s obviously you’re going to develop a new dog or cat food first, then you’re going to develop the packaging, then you’re going to put it out as a promotion, then you’re going to properly launch it, so whenever you’re working on anything it’s not going to happen for a few years and she said it’s quite frustrating when you’ve done all this work and then maybe the business hasn’t got enough money to carry it on any more or, you know, you never know and you just have – you know, if someone turns round and says, ‘This project isn’t running any more’ you’d have to get on with it, you can’t go, ‘Oh no, please can you carry it on, I’ve put some work into it’. Um, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do the company have a structure or programme in place for the placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It’s like, um, you’re supposed to have, like, because there’s a lot of us over all the sites, there’s 50 of us all together, um, so every month we’re supposed to have something. So like last month we went to [place] which is one of the other sites and they – the students there told us what they did, showed us around their site and, um, like next month instead of a visit next month we’re having a presentation skills training, and there’s always – there’s always like training or a visit somewhere each month and then there’s like, there’s goals along the way. Like, um, in January we’re supposed to have appraisals for our half-year, so we set our targets for the rest of the year and things like that, sort of stop off points.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think those things are a good idea then or do you think they could be improved at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s a good idea because it’s everyone at the moment everyone in the business is going through exactly the same thing so it kind of makes us more included, like we’re the same as everyone else, and it checks that you’re still doing – because I think it’s quite easy to sort of wander off and not – sort of lose direction of what you’re doing, so it checks you’re still on track.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What does your own role in the company involve? What can you tell me about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I can tell you, basically, well, I was in packaging innovation; I'm now in packaging development, so I do similar things. So one of the brands in the business will say, um, ‘We want a new package for this product we’ve got’ and, um, it’ll come to me in innovation, so I just come up with any new crazy ideas that I can, or, you know, different new ways of, um, having a package, and then I normally make prototypes of those packages and maybe take them to consumer testing and then if it’s successful the package would go on and get developed by someone else and, um, hopefully hit the shops.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that’s quite exciting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what you expected you would be doing before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To be honest, I had no idea at all. I came and visited once before I started just for a day, um, well, not even a day, like a couple of hours in the afternoon, just met my manager and had a walk round, which was good, it kind of put my mind at rest a bit, and, um, yeah, so I knew vaguely but they couldn’t, because of this whole confidentiality thing they couldn’t really tell me until I got here what I was going to be doing, but, um, yeah, it’s perfect, it’s absolutely fine, because I feel like I've got – I’m doing a little bit related to the course but it’s nice, it’s not – it’s not the same, it’s like…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, still learning loads of stuff.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely and certainly since my job’s changed, um, like because my new manager’s sort of acquired me, he never went and recruited me like my old manager did, he’s not had a student before and so it’s a lot more real the stuff I'm doing. These are projects that he’s had sat at the side waiting for someone to have time to do them on his team and now he says, ‘Right, well if Rebecca means to come and work for me then this is what she can do’ and it’s really exciting. It’s good. It’s real, it’s like hopefully something you’ll get in the shops.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Wow. Do you feel like the company have been supportive of you then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I had, well like I say, I had some trouble when I was asked to relocate to France, because basically my manager, because she was – she applied for this nine month secondment, they do it within the business so you can change your role just for nine months, and she didn’t tell me she’d applied because she didn’t know if she’d get it or not, but when she got it it was the day before she was going on holiday for three weeks, so she sort of said to me, ‘Oh Rebecca, I need to talk to you quickly’, and sort of said, ‘Right, I’m leaving my job, um, can you have a think about what you’d like to get out of this year and we’ll try and accommodate you. Think about it. Okay, I’m going on holiday’. So I was a bit sort of – a bit lost, didn’t know what to do really for a few weeks and because she went on holiday it was left for three weeks just for me to think about it, and it turned out nothing was getting done and it was just stressing me out quite a lot. And in the end one day I came in and I was like, ‘Oh what’s going on?’ and after that everyone was really supportive and they were like, ‘Look, this is our problem, not yours. It’s our fault she’s leaving, we need to do everything we can to accommodate you’. So we all sat down and I said what the kind of things I wanted to be doing and everyone, like my new manager said, ‘Right, I’ve got this project you could do, which is something you could do’, so they were all really good in the end.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you wish you had said something earlier then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, yeah, definitely. It went on, because there was the whole three weeks she was on holiday, it probably went on for at least another three weeks after that as well, of everyone – I think they were expecting me to say like, ‘This is what I want to do’, either go to France or stay in England, and I was waiting for them to say, ‘Right, this is how we’ll help you to make your decision’. No one was actually doing anything, so it’s definitely something I’ve learnt is, you know, I just need to get on with it and say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve really enjoyed it. And before I wasn’t sure like I haven’t been – obviously I’ve only been here six months or so, but before I didn’t know what I wanted to do after I graduate but I’m definitely thinking now that I’ll apply for the graduate training scheme, because I’ve just really enjoyed – I don’t mean necessarily here, but just the whole like structured thing and I feel like I’ve learnt so much anyway I wouldn’t mind going straight into a job and doing a similar thing after university.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What have been the best and worst things about the placement so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, so the worst thing was the sort of upheaval, expected to move to France or whatever, but the best thing has been I feel like I’ve got real responsibility and my project’s real and I’ve – I’ve been able to travel quite a lot, which I wasn’t even expecting, so… I’ve been to Holland and I’ve been to Germany and, um, I’ve been lots of places around the UK as well, so it’s really nice. It’s like – I feel like I’ve just learnt a lot just from doing that, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Excellent. Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, well, one thing I’ve got to do is my dissertation and I haven’t thought what I’m going to write it on or anything like that, so that’s something I’ve got to do soon, obviously I haven’t done so far. But, um, apart from the whole experience of things I just feel like I’ve learnt so much already I’d quite happily walk out tomorrow and, you know, be happy with what I’ve learnt, because just the whole, just being here and getting involved in everything I think it just – it’s really helped.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that there are any drawbacks at all to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I really can’t think of any. I mean like some of my friends are in their final – final year now doing my course and she said to me that just the people who come back from placement are just totally separate from everyone else and they just – they just get on, and she’s a really conscientious girl or she’s always the most conscientious person I’ve ever known, she just said that you can just see they’re so used to being in work and stuff they just get on with everything, like they just – they’re totally separate and they don’t mix with the other people because no one can understand – everyone’s going ‘Oh we’re just going back to bed for another two hours and then we’ll start this project’ and they’re having meetings, and she said, ‘Oh, you’re going to find it so useful next year’ and, you know, she said that as someone who would never have done a placement, but she said that to me, so… It just – I can’t – I just feel like it will help me so much if I’m going to go for graduate schemes as well. I feel like I know so much more about business and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’d recommend other people go on placement or whatever?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, probably like some of my skills have changed. Um, like I found when I first started I found it quite hard to like ring up people in other countries and just be like, ‘Oh hi, I'm Rebecca’ and start chatting to them, but you’re just expected to and that was something my first manager sort of gave me feedback on. She was like, ‘You’ve just got to get on with it and ring them up’ and so I think I’m probably a bit more confident and, um, but like socially we’re still students really, we all live together and we still act like students, so it’s kind of – it’s probably like that I haven’t changed much, but, um…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you moved here as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. So there’s nine of us who are placement students living here. We’ve got two houses, we live next door to each other, so it’s kind of – it’s kind of like being students, which is nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that you are treated as equally as the other placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s difficult because we’re all doing different jobs and so like you’ve spoken to [name] and [name] who are on the same course as me but we do totally different things here and, um, I feel – I just think I’ve been quite lucky because – because like I say, everyone else’s managers have had students before but my manager hasn’t and so he’s treating me more like, um, an associate, so that’s why I’ve got to travel – travel and stuff, because, um, he doesn’t realise he shouldn’t spend that much money on me. So it’s probably – it’s hard to compare how we’re treated. Everyone is – everyone – hopefully everyone enjoys it but we’re all doing such different things it’s really hard to compare.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that you’re probably treated more like a permanent member of staff than the other students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I feel – I wouldn’t say more than the other ones, but like with the projects that I’m doing it’s more necessary for me to travel than it is for, say, [name] because she does a lot of laboratory work here, whereas I need to visit suppliers or whatever and they might be abroad, but that’s my project and her project doesn’t entail that so she doesn’t – but maybe I don’t know, because she doesn’t – it might seem to her like, um, oh I get to go on all these trips but it’s because it’s related to my project, it’s not because I'm more important than her at all. Like we’re all equal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. Have you found it an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely an advantage, it’s really nice. It’s like it’s so nice to have everyone in the same situation and just have – obviously you get on with everyone in your team and stuff, but to have other people the same age as you and, um, you know, to go and meet up with at lunch time and to find out what they’re doing and… if there are other people you can ask them questions without like feeling stupid, because we’re all in the same situation so… and obviously to live with and just to socialise with it’s nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you had to do much team work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, um, when I first started working here we were in – there was just really a team of two of us and I worked alongside my manager pretty much all the time. So, we’d design things and then we’d make the models together, just like work together pretty much all the time. And with this new project, um, I’m working more by myself, I’m not so much supervised, but I’ve had to go to lots of different members of the business, like all over the country – all over Europe and get like their expertise on different areas because obviously they know, they’ve been here a lot longer than me and they know more about different areas, so yeah, I think I’ve had to do quite a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you describe your overall experiences of group work, kind of good or bad?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s really useful for me because, like I say, I’ve been here six months and you’re never going to – as much – as hard as you try you’re never going to learn everything about the business, so, um, just people, they’re just really helpful really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone that you’ve particularly liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no, everyone’s been really nice. I think the thing that I’ve found is that no one will help you unless you sort of help them back. So you can’t just send someone an email and ask them to do some research for you or whatever; you need to say, ‘This is what I’ve found out, hopefully it will help your project’ and then ‘Can you help me with this?’ I think that’s quite important to do because everyone’s so busy they don’t have time just to answer everyone’s questions, they like to get – the like to see something or, you know, be updated on what you’re doing or whatever just to – before they help you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. How do you think that teamwork in the work place compares to teamwork at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s quite different because, um, definitely at uni you’ve already met – you know everyone, whereas here quite often you’ve got to ring someone up and you’ve got to talk to them when you’ve never even met them and you’ve got to have a relationship without meeting them for ages or have a relationship over a video conference or whatever. It’s not – it’s quite different, but I mean the same – I think working together’s the same, it’s just you’re not so familiar with each other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. Have you got a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that having a mentor’s a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know. I think – I think the reason that I’ve got him is supposed to be for, um, if I’ve got a problem with my own manager that I’m supposed to go and talk to him. But I’ve found that because I’ve spent so much more time with people on my team and stuff he’s not actually in my team, but I actually just never go and talk to him because I’d rather talk to people who I know. So, it’s a nice idea to have someone to go to, but I think you’ve got to have – you’ve got – I should have really made an effort to meet him and get to know him rather than wait until something crops up and then go and see him because it’s just like talking to anyone really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you say that even though you’ve got an official mentor you treat the other people in your team as mentors?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, definitely. Like when, um, I was supposed to be going to France and stuff, I spoke to my official mentor once and that was the first time I’d ever spoken to him because (inaudible) the business and I spoke to people on my team like every day almost, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What do you think are the benefits and drawbacks of having a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, like the drawbacks for me is I kind of get mixed signals because he’s on a similar – like because your mentor’s supposed to be someone who’s on a sort of similar level to your manger, so obviously he knows like the business and he’s quite high up and so he’s sort of like, ‘Oh well I think’, you know, I’ll show him my project and stuff, ‘Oh I think this would be a good idea’ when, you know, you’ve already got direction from someone else. So you kind of get mixed signals a bit, but it is nice to have someone to go to if you need to, like, you know, because my manager travels quite a lot, if he’s not here then I will go to my mentor and just run things past him just because I know he’s got experience and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know, because we get – sometimes we get spoken to by like really high people who are high up in the company, which is, I suppose it’s supposed to like inspire us, but it doesn’t really inspire me because they just seem to work really hard and yeah, they like earn a load of money, but I just sort of think it’s not really worth it if you’re going to be working like 24/7. So, I don’t really look up to them. It’s nice, I think it’s – definitely if you’re going to do something you enjoy it’s nice to get high up in a business or whatever, but I just wouldn’t bother if it’s too much work. Like life’s too short.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Has anyone from uni been to visit you yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, in work?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, a tutor? Yeah, he has.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they tell you what the purpose of the visit was?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, he’s a bit of a strange man. He came in and he filled – he checked we were writing log books, which we’re supposed to be doing, um, but he met – there’s six of us here from [university], he just met us all at once. We all just sat – we sat round a table in one of these rooms. He basically just asked what we were doing, whether we liked our jobs or not, if we did it was fine, if we didn’t, well, he said, ‘Well, just get on with it because it’s a good experience’ and then he went home.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, if you did have any problems would you be happy to go to him?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. He wouldn’t bother. Certainly, like I think some people just said a few things about how they weren’t doing jobs very related to their courses or whatever and he just said, ‘Well, my first job was on a ship where I had to work 12 hours of the day, blah, blah, blah. So don’t ever say you’ve got it bad, just get on with it.’

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it didn’t feel like he was very supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is there anyone else that you’d go to at uni if you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, my tutor’s quite nice, but I think at the end of the day there’s not really – I can’t really – I wouldn’t really expect University to do anything. It’s kind of if I’m at work it’s my problem here and, you know, if I was going to leave the job then I’d leave the job, you know, without – you know, if I felt that strongly about the job then I wouldn’t worry about the University getting involved, I’d just get on with it myself, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you know if uni or here have a complaints procedure if you had any serious problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Here have, I don’t know about uni, I presume they have. Like there’s – there’s a lady that we’ve all been introduced to who you can go to here, um, in human resources who you can go and talk to if you’ve got a problem and they’ll try and sort it out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that that should have been like made clearer to you at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably, yeah. I hadn’t even thought of it, to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How to go about finding out about stuff really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Well I presume you’d just contact the placements guy but like I say he’s a bit funny, so… Yeah, it’s not been made clear.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are there appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. Um, like, do you mean sort of like…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Basically, the reason that I’m asking is because we’re interviewing engineers and stuff as well and some of them are working on building sites and there aren’t women’s toilets and they have like safety clothing that doesn’t fit them and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, no, the women’s toilets are really nice and they’ve got like about a million mirrors and they’ve got sofas in them and stuff, so I think we’re treated quite well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have there been any occasions when you think that your gender has determined reactions you’ve got, or the outcome of events or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so. I always worry, well, I don’t worry about my gender, when I go and see suppliers I’m worried I just look really young, because I don’t tell them I’m a student they just get really confused, thinking why am I so young and why I’m there, but I’ve never – I’ve never really thought as gender being – because like there’s people around me who are quite high up who are female it doesn’t ever seem – you’d never think that there’d be an issue really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I think you did mention this earlier, but at the minute do you think that you want a career in design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, I was saying that I want to do like graduate or something, but like what I’m doing at the moment isn’t particularly design and technology and I’d be quite happy just to – and seeing like the different things people do it’s really interesting around the company, so I wouldn’t be applying specifically for design and technology I don’t think. I’d just go for, like the graduate schemes here you do six months in different jobs, you keep switching round, so I think that’s the kind of thing I’d like to do, get a taste of everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed since doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I had no idea what I wanted to do before I started. Um, I still don’t know what – what jobs specifically I’d want to do, but I definitely think it’d be worthwhile me going on a graduate scheme, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it will, but I don’t think it will help my final year at uni because I'm not doing – I feel like I'm getting a bit out of touch with what – the stuff I did at uni. I think it will be hard to go back in there and – for the last year and get motivated again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think you’ll be able to use what you’ve learnt for your final year project or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not. It’s not very – it’s not very related, so that’s why I think I’ll find it hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Okay. Would you work for [company] if they offered you a job when you graduated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. It would depend what it is and where it is and stuff, well, actually I don’t really mind where it is, but it would depend what the job is because there’s so much different stuff going on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If it was similar to what you were doing now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. These are some questions that I asked you in the last interview, just to see if your views have changed at all since working, so what five words would you now use to describe either design and technology generally or specifically what you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay, so I can choose either/or?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Okay, so what I’m doing now is probably easier. So, it’s creative, but it’s not – yeah, so it’s creative, so I’m still being creative, but it’s not like really arty, so that’s not really a word. Um, it’s enlightening because I get to go lots of different places, yeah, so it’s exciting, and I think it’s quite, I guess like broadening because I get to like learn about lots of different things I didn’t learn about before.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so varied?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, varied, yeah. That’s four, so I’ll try and think of another one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s okay if you can’t.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Is that okay?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think now that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated area or can’t you really answer that properly, working here, because it’s quite even?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s, because it’s quite even I don’t think, because definitely when I think, I probably said last time, when I went into university because they don’t have very many females on the course, um, I felt like I kind of just got in by default because they needed more females, but I definitely don’t feel like that here. Like I, you know, they interviewed us fairly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You feel like you’ve got it because you deserve it rather than…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, rather than just coming in because ‘Oh, we need to make up the numbers’, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: More women should be encouraged into?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t – I don’t really see… I don’t think that, no, I don’t think there’s any kind of real problem. It’s probably – it might just be unlucky that there’s more males than females on my team at the moment, but certainly my old manager was female, she’s now left the team so there will have been more. I think it’s kind of swings and roundabouts; I don’t think they need to be particularly encouraged more. Um, I think it’s quite even.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you think there’s any particular reason why the industry generally is quite male dominated but here isn’t so much? Is it the company’s attitude or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I don’t know. Like when I went to Germany last week I came back on, because it was a midweek flight it was obviously a kind of business flight and I was the only female on the whole plane.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Because I really – I noticed that because I wasn’t dressed up very smart and everyone was dressed up smart and they were kind of looking at me like, you know, what are you doing here? And I was just sort of thinking this is quite bizarre because you don’t – you never feel like you’re, um, that things are – I don’t ever really feel like it’s unequal anywhere but then why are there so many businessmen on this plane and just me? I don’t know why that is. I don’t know why it’s male dominated, but maybe it probably all comes down to women looking after kids.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have [company] got equal opportunities policies and I think [name] said you can work like flexible hours and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So that sort of helps, I suppose, with child care issues.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, as far as I know, I think, I mean definitely like the lady on my team is pregnant so she’s been going off to all her appointments and everything, like I think they’re quite flexible, as far as I know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, okay. That’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, brilliant.
